prize_parts.citation: For developing structural methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets, and models of dynamic industries, which transformed empirical industrial organisation and the practice of merger review and antitrust analysis.

statement.case_for: B001 combines a tractable, widely adopted method with a clear path from theory to data. BLP-style random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices, together with the Ericson-Pakes dynamic-oligopoly framework, lets researchers measure market power, merger effects and welfare in real markets. The tools are used in academic work, antitrust and regulation, and they have spread into trade, health, environmental and public economics. The core papers are from the mid-1990s, so three decades of replication, refinement and regulatory use have tested the work. Its known weaknesses, numerical sensitivity and identification, are well documented and have been largely addressed. Almost every member ranked it in the top three, but I do not treat that as evidence of merit. The case rests on originality, breadth of use and durability, which I judge to be at least as strong as for any other shortlisted candidate. Attribution is also comparatively compact: BLP is credited to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes, and Pakes adds the dynamic-games and estimation strand.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the award would honour a toolkit, and some members may see structural IO as methodological craft rather than a discovery. The ballot entry also pools several distinct strands: demand estimation, dynamic games, production-function estimation and the new empirical IO programme. That makes the unit of the prize and the three-name cut contestable. Naming Levinsohn rather than Bresnahan could be read as favouring the single BLP paper over the broader agenda that made it possible. Structural results can also be sensitive to functional-form and equilibrium assumptions.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first but names Bresnahan rather than Levinsohn alongside Pakes and Berry, because Bresnahan pioneered the new empirical IO and early differentiated-products demand estimation. He concedes that reasonable people could swap the two.
responses.response: I take Bresnahan's claim seriously and regard it as the most serious attribution risk in the candidacy. I still keep Levinsohn. The citation I propose is tied to a specific, identifiable contribution, estimating demand with endogenous prices in differentiated-product markets, and that is the BLP paper. Bresnahan's work is more a programme and an agenda. A prize citing the method should name the people who produced it. If the Committee preferred a broader citation on the new empirical IO programme, Bresnahan would belong in it, and I would reconsider the slate then. Krusell and I agree that the structural estimation core is the same.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B013 first. She sees a clear explanatory framework combined with new empirical designs and large policy impact, and she accepts that Dorn's omission under the three-name limit makes attribution contestable.
responses.response: I agree on the quality of the empirical designs and on the policy relevance, and B013 is my clear second choice. I rank it below B001 for two reasons. The China-shock magnitudes and long-run persistence are still debated, which is not true of BLP-type methods after three decades. Credit is also split across two strands, the task and skill-premium framework and the trade-shock evidence, so any three names leave out a central contributor (Dorn, or the task-model authors outside the list). I do not dismiss her point that B013 fits a discovery-plus-framework standard, and I would be comfortable with it as the alternative if B001 stalls.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B002 first. He sees Kiyotaki-Moore collateral amplification and the financial accelerator as a deep, general contribution to macro-finance, while acknowledging overlap with the 2022 prize and the problem of crediting Gertler, Gilchrist and Bernanke.
responses.response: I put B002 third, and the conceptual originality of Kiyotaki-Moore is not in doubt. The difficulty is that the 2022 prize rewarded banks and financial crises, so the Committee must show clearly what is distinct about collateral-constraint amplification. The accelerator strand also runs through Bernanke, who is not on this ballot entry. Empirical identification of the collateral channel is less clean than the theory suggests. B001 has no comparable overlap or attribution problem, and no prior prize recognises this structural estimation tradition. If the Committee wants a macro-finance award, I would support the clean Kiyotaki-Moore pair, with Gertler's inclusion open to argument.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B001 first and B049 second. He regards nominal rigidities and rule-based monetary policy as hugely influential, but sees the credit as crowded, so any trio leaves out important contributors.
responses.response: I agree that the influence of the New Keynesian framework is very large, and I accept his point that B001's timing is ripe. I do not rank B049 in my top eight because of the attribution problem he identifies. Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets all have strong claims, and I do not see a defensible three-person cut. The framework's performance in the 2021–23 inflation also remains debated. B001's attribution is much more compact, which is a real advantage given the three-laureate limit.

uncertainties: Whether Bresnahan should replace Levinsohn, and how the Committee would weigh the new empirical IO programme against the specific BLP contribution.
Whether the Committee treats the work as a discovery or as a methodological toolkit, and how that affects its standing against substantive-finding candidates.
Whether a single-achievement configuration is best, or whether a second achievement could be added within the three-person limit without weakening the citation.
I rely on background knowledge and have not independently verified citation or adoption counts.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in corporate finance and private equity, and my listed co-authors (Kaplan, Axelson, Weisbach and others) are not candidates on the shortlist. I am an adjunct professor at Chicago Booth, but I see no link to a shortlisted candidate. I work close to B012, but B001 is my first choice and I tried to apply the common criteria.
